newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan human rights group says abuses rose in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Jordan human rights group says abuses rose in 1996.

text.p: A Jordanian human rights group said on Wednesday it registered increases last year in complaints of abuse including torture, arrest without charges and denial of freedom of expression.

The Arab Organisation for Human Rights (AOHR) in Jordan said in its annual report that government intolerance of opposition to economic reform and a security crackdown following August bread riots were the main causes of the rise in complaints.

It said respect for human rights had declined during 1996 despite pledges from the government of Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti when it was formed last year of greater accountability and openness.

"The organisation received many complaints and testimonies of torture, which is unacceptable and impossible to stay silent about," the report said, citing complaints of severe beatings, pulling out of toenails and moustaches, and threats of rape.
The government denies reports of torture and has challenged the AOHR to provide physical or medical evidence to back up its claims.

The 1996 U.S. State Department report on human rights in Jordan said torture reports were difficult to verify but that "security and other police forces abuse detainees physically during interrogation."

The AOHR also called for reform of Jordan's penal code to cancel a law against slandering King Hussein or Jordan's royal family -- a crime known as lese-majeste. It said the law was an all-encompassing charge used to detain citizens without trial.
It said seven people were serving sentences of up to three years for lese-majeste, which the government says is a security issue rather than a political charge.
"Throughout Jordan's history there has never been such a large number of cases of lese-majeste," the report said.
Between 20 and 25 journalists were taken to court in 1996 over newspaper articles, reflecting a serious threat to freedom of expression, it said.
"Opposition to the government's political and economic programme led to a clear decline in the readiness of the government to accept an alternative view," the report said.

In its few first months in office Kabariti's government promoted closer ties with Israel despite continued public unease over a 1994 peace treaty with the Jewish state, distancing Jordan from Iraq, its biggest trading partner, and cutting grain subsidies, a move which sparked rioting in the south in August.

Government officials say there were no political charges filed against journalists and all were the result of publishing slander, articles threatening national security or offending the country's conservative morals.

But the AOHR report drew comparisons between human rights under Kabariti's government and the years before 1989, when King Hussein instigated a widespread democratisation process in Jordan to end martial law.

"Even though the start of the year witnessed the formation of a new Jordanian government which announced its commitment to maintaining freedoms and rights of Jordanians...(events) led to a collapse of human rights and to many negative practices which brought to mind the period of martial law," it said.
